KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Low pressure south of Long Island, NY will scoot ENE this
morning with steady rain largely coming to an end by day break.
Mesoscale models are in good agreement that skies will be mostly
sunny south of the mountains today while areas north of the
mountains may remain mostly cloudy as a back door cold front
approaches. It will be mild today with highs mainly in the 60s
with spots south of the mountains making a run into the low 70s.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

A back door cold front will march SSW through the area late
today into Tuesday morning with high pressure building over the
Canadian Maritimes. This high will be well positioned to set up
cold air damming across the area Tuesday as an area of low
pressure tracks east out of the Great Lakes. This low will move
overhead Tuesday night and then offshore Wednesday morning.
There is some subtle variability in the track of the low 
amongst guidance which will impact the swath of heaviest QPF as 
well as thermal profiles across the mountains and areas near the
Canadian border in Maine. Latest guidance suggests a swath of +1
inches of QPF will be possible with a multi model consensus
placing that swath from the White Mountains towards the Mid
Coast and points north. To the south amounts drop off with far
southern NH forecast to receive less than a quarter of an inch.

It will be a cold rain for much of the area with highs mainly in
the 40s while thermal profiles in the mountains and points
northeast may support a period of wintry precipitation during
the day Tuesday. Around Jackman, ME profiles from the 00Z HRRR
suggest the column will be cool enough for snow Tuesday morning
with a transition to a wintry mix and then rain Tuesday evening.
Farther to the SW profiles from the HRRR show a warm nose aloft
with a sub-freezing layer generally between 6,000 feet and 1,500
feet. This would support freezing rain near mountain summits
while valleys above 1,500 feet may see more in the way of sleet.
As the low moves overhead Tuesday night profiles will likely
warm enough for mainly rain with precipitation tapering off late
Tuesday night into Wednesday morning.


KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
Low pressure exits off to the east on Wednesday with a trailing
front bring as end to the precipitation as it does. It looks 
like the system has become more progressive, and most of the 
area should be dry by early morning. The Midcoast will likely be
the last to clear later in the morning. Skies look to end up 
mostly sunny to partly cloudy south of the mountains by peak 
heating, so guidance suggests temperatures climb into the mid 
to upper 60s (and maybe even into the low 70s for southern New 
Hampshire). Northwesterly flow is going to keep clouds and 
showers banked up to the terrain so temperatures hang more in 
the 50s to near 60F. As showers continue into the night some of 
the higher elevations may see some light snow, but the clouds 
are going to keep lower elevations above freezing. Warmer 850 mb
temperatures move in with the ridging aloft, so while south of 
the mountains sees mostly clear skies temperatures still only 
fall into the low to mid 40s.

The aforementioned low pressure system continues to deepen as 
it moves over the Canadian Maritimes on Thursday, which tightens
the pressure gradient between it and the high pressure building
in to our west. It is going to be a breezy day for sure with 
northwesterly wind gusts 25-35 mph, but guidance suggests we 
could tap into the 50kt low level jet aloft and see wind gusts 
near 40 mph at times. This is going to have to continue to be 
watched as positioning of the jet is going to make the 
difference and guidance has been trending in more eastward, but 
again confidence in wind gusts at least up to 35 mph is high.

We could see a rinse and repeat solution Friday and Saturday as
another low pressure system takes a similar track to the first 
one, but the difference is that models have been pretty 
consistently depicting this one being stronger. Widespread rain
is likely Friday into Saturday , but that is all I am willing 
to say about that at this point. What catches my eye more is the
signal for potentially strong winds Saturday if this low bombs 
out in the proximity of Nova Scotia like most global models are 
depicting. The European and Canadian model have been especially 
bullish showing widespread 40+ mph gusts. The GFS doesn't quite 
show the strengthening the others do and therefore suggests a 
solution more similar to the Tuesday system. We will see how 
things trend, but a signal like that bears watching.
